claims.proposition_evaluated: The City's latest published condition ratings available by September 3, 2026 show that its published Roads asset class was in poor condition as of the inventory date those ratings describe.
claims.interpretation_notes: Partially supported. Appendix B reports 11.2% Poor (D&F) for the City-named Roads class by replacement value, above the brief's 10% partial threshold and below its 25% supported threshold. The alternative 7.5% and 20% cutoffs also yield Partially supported. The report was presented January 21, 2026 and describes assets as of December 31, 2024; it cannot establish their condition in August 2026. Roads includes Paved Roads, Unpaved Roads and Curbs. Its published 2023 comparator was 11.4% D&F, but changed reporting and class composition prevent a like-for-like trend claim. Bridges, sidewalks, streetlights, transit, buildings and parks are separate classes and are excluded.

supporting_evidence.finding: Appendix B gives Roads replacement value of C$10,484,313,206 and a condition distribution of 70.8% Good (A&B), 16.2% Fair (C), 11.2% Poor (D&F), and 1.7% Not Rated. Paved Roads are 12.5% D&F, Unpaved Roads are 100% Not Rated, and Curbs are 7.0% D&F.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 2025 Infrastructure State and Condition, Appendix B, page 37
supporting_evidence.establishes: The published Roads-class result and all three nested rows on the replacement-value denominator.

supporting_evidence.finding: The report says replacement value weights the portfolio attributes and identifies the underlying inventory date as December 31, 2024.

challenging_evidence.finding: The same Roads row reports 70.8% Good (A&B) and 11.2% Poor (D&F), well below the brief's 25% threshold for Supported.
challenging_evidence.source_title: 2025 Infrastructure State and Condition, Appendix B, page 37
challenging_evidence.establishes: Why the proposition's generality does not meet the Supported band.

limitations: Appendix B groups A with B and D with F, so it does not publish five separate grades for the Roads class. The four published groups are reported in full above.
The table gives asset quantities with varying units, but no Roads-class condition distribution by kilometres or lane-kilometres. The required length-based alternative cannot be classified.
The 2023 Roads row reports 11.4% D&F, but the 2025 report changed its organization and identifies Curbs separately under Roads. The 0.2-point difference is not evidence of improvement.

The City's older capital budget states a Council target of fewer than 10% of arterial roads in D or F condition. That narrower arterial target cannot classify the full Roads class by replacement value.

The open-data renewal dataset and its map did not expose their field lists or last-updated dates through this reviewer's tools. Their renewal schedules cannot substitute for an alley condition distribution.
unknowns: The condition of any particular street and whether the Roads-class share changed after December 31, 2024.
The share of Roads assets newly assessed in the latest inventory rather than carried forward.
A published, current A-to-F distribution for alleys as a separate asset class was not located in the condition-report materials or accessible open-data catalogue.

missing_evidence.description: Accessible field lists and update metadata for the Neighbourhood and Alley Renewal dataset and derived map, plus any separately published alley A-to-F inventory.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton Open Data and Integrated Infrastructure Services

calculations_needed: Primary Roads-class p=11.2% D&F by replacement value: Partially supported under both cutoff sets.

The adopted CM-27-0000 alley-renewal profile says 63% (764 km) of paved alleys require renewal and states a Council-approved goal of Fair or better alley condition by 2043. The 63% is a renewal-need share, not an A-to-F condition rating and not an alley verdict. https://www.edmonton.ca/sites/default/files/public-files/2023-2026CapitalBudget.pdf
what_would_change_my_verdict: A City correction or eligible later report available by the freeze date putting the published Roads-class D&F replacement-value share below 10% or at least 25%.
A published Roads-class length distribution in another band would make the finding definition-sensitive, though the brief's primary verdict would still use replacement value.
claims.suggested_one_line: The City's January 2026 report rates 11.2% of its Roads class poor or very poor by replacement value in an inventory dated December 31, 2024—a substantial minority under this review's thresholds.

claims.proposition_evaluated: At least half of the $100 million council approved for CM-20-0330 came from funding sources that permitted road or alley renewal instead.
claims.interpretation_notes: Supported under both cutoff sets. The adopted profile and council motion identify the whole $100 million as Tax-Supported Debt, which the brief expressly treats as eligible general municipal capital funding unless a restriction is shown. E=$100.0 million, X=$0 and U=$0 for the original approval. A later project-specific borrowing bylaw governs use after approval; it does not establish that Council lacked the earlier allocation choice. This source-eligibility finding does not predict what Council would have approved instead or establish a transfer into bike lanes from road renewal.

supporting_evidence.finding: The adopted profile lists Tax-Supported Debt as the only approved funding source, with C$5.950 million in 2023, C$26.750 million in 2024, C$33.650 million in 2025 and C$33.650 million in 2026, totaling C$100.000 million. The source table prints in thousands.
supporting_evidence.establishes: The funding source and annual amounts for every dollar of the original approval.

supporting_evidence.finding: Council's December 2022 minutes record approval of the $100 million profile with funding from Tax-Supported Debt.
supporting_evidence.source_title: City Council budget deliberations, post-meeting minutes
supporting_evidence.establishes: The adopted motion and source, distinct from withdrawn and defeated alternatives.

supporting_evidence.finding: The Spring 2025 adjustment transferred C$430,000 of tax-supported debt out of CM-20-0330 to the Dunluce Neighbourhood and Alley Renewal profile. A later profile sheet shows CM-20-0330's current approved total as C$99.570 million, still all Tax-Supported Debt.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Spring 2025 Supplemental Capital Budget Adjustment, Attachment 4; CM-20-0330 profile
supporting_evidence.establishes: The identified later approved reduction and its destination.

challenging_evidence.finding: Bylaw 20394 subsequently authorized borrowing for the specified active-transportation project, constraining use under that authorization after Council's allocation. It does not identify an externally restricted grant or negate the original source eligibility.
challenging_evidence.establishes: The later project-specific authorization and its timing.

challenging_evidence.finding: The City says the C$430,000 moved to Dunluce funded active-transportation connections along adjacent arterial roads; the destination profile's renewal name alone does not prove that sum paid for road or alley surface renewal.
challenging_evidence.establishes: The purpose of the reverse transfer and the limit of an inference from the profile name.

limitations: The funding-source verdict tests the December 2022 $100 million approval. Subsequent profile reductions do not retroactively change that approval.

The June 2025 transfer went to a profile whose published split is 9% growth and 91% renewal, but the City specifies active-transportation connections as the use of these particular dollars. Applying the destination profile's aggregate split to the C$430,000 would invent an allocation.

No complete transfer-by-transfer audit of every 2023–2026 adjustment through September 3, 2026 was independently completed. The identified C$430,000 reduction is corroborated by later C$99.570 million profile totals.
No restricted grant is identified for CM-20-0330, so grant eligibility terms are not implicated.
unknowns: Whether any adjustment not located in the reviewed records affected CM-20-0330 after the June 2025 reduction.
Whether another council record identifies a transfer from a renewal-funded allocation into CM-20-0330; none was established here.

missing_evidence.description: A consolidated, transfer-by-transfer review of all capital adjustments through September 3, 2026, including each source profile's published growth/renewal split.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton Financial and Corporate Services

calculations_needed: Original approved amount, in nominal C$ millions: 2023 5.950; 2024 26.750; 2025 33.650; 2026 33.650; total 100.000. The adopted table prints C$ thousands.
Original-source classification: E=100.000, X=0, U=0, so Supported at the primary C$50 million and alternative C$25 million thresholds.

Identified approved adjustment: June 10, 2025, C$0.430 million from CM-20-0330 to 25-25-9506; subsequent City profile sheets show C$99.570 million approved. The City describes the transferred work as active-transportation connections, not road or alley surface renewal. https://pub-edmonton.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=261605 https://pub-edmonton.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=276900

Located year-end cumulative actuals, in C$ millions: 2023 0.807 and 2024 10.496, giving 2024 expenditure of 10.496−0.807=9.689. The reported 2025 cumulative actual of 39.984 would give 2025 expenditure of 39.984−10.496=29.488, but the 2025 City attachment could not be independently opened and that final figure remains provisional. https://pub-edmonton.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=219748 https://pub-edmonton.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=252513 https://pub-edmonton.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=291480
what_would_change_my_verdict: A controlling restriction showing that more than C$50 million of the original Tax-Supported Debt could not have funded road or alley renewal.
A corrected adopted funding table identifying enough restricted or undetermined dollars to reduce E below C$50 million.
claims.suggested_one_line: The adopted budget funded all $100 million with Tax-Supported Debt, a source eligible for road or alley renewal under this review's rule; that establishes an available funding choice, not what Council would have chosen.

claims.proposition_evaluated: The $100 million approved for bike lanes equalled a serious share of the City's published infrastructure renewal shortfall for the same 2023–2026 capital cycle.
claims.interpretation_notes: Partially supported under both cutoff sets. The latest located City figure covering 2023–2026 is an approximately C$1.52 billion renewal investment shortfall. C$100 million divided by C$1.52 billion is about 6.58%, within the primary 5% to below 25% band and the alternative 3% to below 15% band. The adopted budget's original 'Renewal Funding Gap' was C$1.63 billion, yielding about 6.13% and the same classification. The two figures are different budget vintages, not different time spans. The 2027–2030 and ten-year gaps are excluded from classification. Magnitude does not establish that funds could be moved; Claim 2 addresses source eligibility.

supporting_evidence.finding: The City's 2024 Financial Annual Report states that the renewal investment shortfall in 2023–2026 is approximately C$1.52 billion.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 2024 Financial Annual Report, Asset Renewal Investment, page 53
supporting_evidence.establishes: A later City-published whole-infrastructure shortfall for the numerator's four-year period.

supporting_evidence.finding: The June 2025 council report says C$110.8 million had been added through supplemental adjustments for unfunded renewal, leaving an approximately C$1.52 billion 2023–2026 renewal investment shortfall.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Prioritization of Renewal in 2027–2030 Capital Budget, FCS02696, page 3
supporting_evidence.establishes: The same-period updated City figure and why it differs from the adopted budget's gap.

supporting_evidence.finding: The adopted budget gives C$3,575.584 million of 'RIMS Ideal Investment' and C$1,945.673 million of 'Funded RIMS Ideal Investment' for 2023–2026, and calls their rounded difference the C$1.63 billion 'Renewal Funding Gap.' It separately reports C$2,194.927 million of total funded renewal.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Adopted 2023–2026 Capital Budget, Renewal Funding Gap, Tables 5 and 6, pages 48–49
supporting_evidence.establishes: The original requirement, funded amount, difference, City terminology and distinction between total funded renewal and the amount counted against the modelled ideal.

challenging_evidence.finding: Even against the later, smaller C$1.52 billion shortfall, C$100 million is only about 6.58%, below the brief's 25% threshold for a serious share.
challenging_evidence.source_title: 2024 Financial Annual Report, Asset Renewal Investment, page 53
challenging_evidence.establishes: The scale that prevents a Supported verdict.

limitations: C$1.52 billion is expressly approximate; 6.58% is arithmetic on that rounded City figure.
No City-published 2023–2026 roads-and-alleys-only renewal shortfall was established. The required narrower alternative therefore has no classification.
The adopted C$1.63 billion gap uses the RIMS ideal-funded line, not the larger C$2.194927 billion total funded renewal line. Substituting the latter would change the City's stated basis.

The City's approximately 54% originally funded and later approximately 57.5% funded rates describe investment levels; neither is a published benchmark for what constitutes a serious share of the shortfall.
No City-published renewal unit cost sufficient to state what C$100 million buys in road kilometres or completed neighbourhoods was established.
unknowns: Whether a City publication available by September 3, 2026 gives a still later revised 2023–2026 shortfall than the located C$1.52 billion figure.
A separately published same-period roads-and-alleys renewal gap.
A City benchmark for the desired percentage of its whole-infrastructure renewal requirement funded in this cycle.

missing_evidence.description: A City-defined 2023–2026 roads-and-alleys-only renewal requirement and funded amount, if one was published.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton Financial and Corporate Services and Integrated Infrastructure Services

calculations_needed: Latest located same-period comparison: C$100 million / approximately C$1,520 million = 0.06579, about 6.58%; Partially supported under primary and alternative cutoffs.

Adopted-budget comparison: C$3,575.584 million ideal minus C$1,945.673 million funded RIMS ideal = C$1,629.911 million, rounded by the City to a C$1.63 billion Renewal Funding Gap; C$100 million / C$1,630 million = about 6.13%, also Partially supported.

The adopted budget describes its whole capital budget as approximately C$7.9 billion, so C$100 million was about 1.27% of that rounded adopted amount. It was about 4.56% of the C$2,194.927 million total funded renewal reported in Table 5. These are supplementary shares, not shortfall verdict ratios.

The C$4.8 billion gap for 2023–2032 would give 2.08%, but its ten-year span differs from the four-year numerator and it is unclassified. https://www.gov.edmonton.ab.ca/sites/default/files/public-files/2024FinancialAnnualReport.pdf
what_would_change_my_verdict: A controlling same-period City shortfall of C$400 million or less would make the primary ratio at least 25% and the verdict Supported.
A controlling same-period City shortfall above C$2 billion would put the primary ratio below 5% and make the verdict Contradicted.
Evidence that no published City shortfall covers 2023–2026 would require Not established under the brief's period rule.
claims.suggested_one_line: The City's later report puts its 2023–2026 renewal shortfall at about $1.52 billion; the $100 million bike-lane approval equals roughly 6.6% of it, a partial share under the brief's thresholds.
